title: Goat and sheep horns form a series of homologous spirals of increasing angle

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Goat and sheep horns form a series of homologous spirals of increasing angle

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Horns of wild goats and sheep form a series of homologous logarithmic spirals with increasing constant angle: under 40° in Oryx, under 70° in the Scinde wild goat, about 75° in Ovis ammon and a little more in the Highland ram.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: we may easily arrange a series of forms, such for example as the Siberian ibex, the moufflon, _Ovis Ammon_, etc., and ending with the long-horned Highland ram: in which, as we pass from one to another, we recognise precisely homologous spirals, with an increasing angular constant, the spiral angle being, for instance, about 75° or rather less in _Ovis Ammon_, and in the Highland ram a very little more.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Spiral angle of horns”. Scope: horns of Oryx, Capra and Ovis species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-04: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.80

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The named taxa, numerical angles and predicted ordering make this directly falsifiable. Public museum collections should provide enough specimens for a practical comparative test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit species-specific logarithmic spiral angles to standardized horn centerlines for the named Oryx, Capra and Ovis taxa and test the stated ordering and approximate values. Nonlogarithmic fits, angles outside uncertainty bounds or a reversed ordering would refute the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Photographic perspective requires calibration or 3D records.

Sex, age and subspecies can alter horn geometry.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.62
data existence: 0.74
analysis feasibility: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.9
operationalizability: 0.95

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is a short ordered list of angles, so it is highly decidable once homologous measurements exist. Museum media cover these animals, but they are not a ready-made morphometric table, and several of the horns are photographed rather than scanned. A small team could measure a modest series from images, with real uncertainty in the angle definition for horns that also twist out of plane.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate the constant spiral angle of horn sheaths of Oryx, the Sindh wild goat, Ovis ammon, and Highland sheep from calibrated photographs or scans, using the same fitting convention on each. The series claim is confirmed if the angles rise in that order and fall near the stated bounds (under 40°, under 70°, about 75°, and slightly higher); overlap or a reversed order would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The named forms are not all present as metrically calibrated open 3D sheaths.

Spiral angle on a helical horn depends on how the plane of the generating spiral is chosen.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.86
discriminating power: 0.76
data existence: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.58
data adequacy: 0.42
